Researchers have found a new way to shrink massive computer learning models without losing their smarts [P3_p1_c02]. Training many different computer models together gives great results, but using them all at once is too slow and expensive for everyday users [P3_p1_c02]. 

To solve this, scientists use a method called distillation [P3_p1_c03]. Like insects that change form as they grow, computer systems can use a large, heavy model for heavy-duty learning, and then transfer that knowledge into a small model that runs fast [P3_p1_c03]. 

The big idea is to train the small model to mimic the soft probabilities of the large model, rather than just copying final hard answers [P3_p2_c04]. This passes along rich details about how different categories relate to one another [P3_p2_c04]. 

The results are striking. More than 80% of the accuracy gains achieved by a bulky group of 10 models can be successfully squeezed into a single distilled model [P3_p5_c02]. Scientists also introduced specialist models that focus on fine details and learn rapidly in parallel [P3_p1_c02]. 

This matters because it makes advanced artificial intelligence much easier to deploy to a large number of users without needing massive computing power [P3_p1_c02].
